description: We are interested in connecting with the reality that astronauts experience in space, through documentary-style analysis presented via the mechanics and storytelling of a video game.
summary:
Hubble: Repair in Orbit is a documentary-style browser game about STS-61 (December 1993), the first Hubble servicing mission. Playing as the repair crew, you perform simplified EVA tasks — swapping a Rate Sensing Unit, replacing a solar array, installing WFPC2 and COSTAR — using one deliberate control grammar: align, hold, release, verify. Precision replaces reflexes: the game teaches how astronauts work slowly and carefully in vacuum.

Every step is grounded in primary sources: NASA mission history, the oral history of astronaut Jeffrey Hoffman, and 1993 mission fact sheets. Real archival footage and photographs (including the released solar array drifting over Earth) interrupt gameplay at key moments, essay-film style, connecting each action to what actually happened.

The game runs entirely in the browser (HTML5, Three.js/WebGL), works offline as a single file, and is fully bilingual: English interface with Spanish narration and subtitles in both languages. It is accessible by keyboard, with reduced-motion support and no time pressure.

Play it, fail safely, repeat — and learn why rehearsing underwater for a year mattered when seven astronauts had five spacewalks to save the most famous telescope in history.
details:
What does it do? It lets anyone experience, step by step, what it took to repair the Hubble Space Telescope in orbit. Across five episodes mirroring the real five EVAs of STS-61, players secure their feet, align tools, apply controlled force, and verify their work — always at their own pace, with no time pressure or fail states.

How does it work? It is a single self-contained HTML file that runs in any modern browser (WebGL2 via Three.js). Tasks use one consistent control grammar: arrows to align, holding Space to act, releasing to stop, Enter to verify. A fixed-camera, shot-based presentation (inspired by the essay-film style of Chris Marker) alternates playable sequences with real archival photographs and footage — including the released solar array drifting above Earth. Sound is interpretive: an underwater ambience for training, suit-and-radio ambience for orbital work.

What benefits does it have? It makes orbital servicing — a topic usually told through headlines — tangible and teachable. It is bilingual (English interface, Spanish narration, subtitles in both), keyboard-accessible, reduced-motion friendly, works offline, and labels every simplification: players always know what is documented history versus stylized recreation.

What do you hope to achieve? To show that precision, patience and training — not reflexes — are what spacewalking demands, and to inspire curiosity about humanity's most famous repair mission using primary sources players can explore themselves.

What tools did you use? HTML5, CSS, JavaScript (ES modules), Three.js r180 with GLTFLoader/DRACOLoader, gltf-transform for model optimization, esbuild bundling, Web Audio API for synthesized ambience, and Playwright for automated keyboard-testing of every mission path. 3D assets include team-supplied models (RSU, solar arrays, PRT) plus instrument geometry extracted from the team's Hubble model. Archival images and video: team-supplied material with NASA mission context cited in-game. Ambient sounds: freesound.org (TommasoMotteran; Col. Chris Hadfield).
